articles.text: On January 27, city staff announced that they would bring the Housing Element to City Council for adoption after the state’s 90-day review period, which ends on February 16. Adoption is expected in late February or March. The state deadline for Housing Element adoption was January 31; and cities not meeting the deadline face the “Builder’s Remedy.” This is a clause added to California’s Housing Accountability Act in 1990 by which developers can file an application for a housing development which does not comply with a city’s local zoning laws, if the city has not passed its Housing Element. Any housing development applied for under the Builder’s Remedy must have 20% of its units available to lower-income households, or all its units available to middle-income households or transitional or supportive housing. However, state building limitations still hold — most pertinently the California Environmental Quality Act, a statute passed in 1970 by then-governor Ronald Reagan which limits proposed building projects on the grounds of potentially “significant environmental effects.” “Generally,” said Planning & Building Director Kevin Jackson, “[the Builder’s Remedy] is a tool used by developers in cities where there are sites ready to go, where somebody has been working on a project for a while and now they have their opportunity to push it forward. It’s not really that useful for properties that have no developer interests, because it takes time to figure out what kind of project makes sense.” Under the Builder’s Remedy, any noncompliant city is also ineligible for state grants and funding for road repair and infrastructure. articles.text: In preparation for African American History Month this year, I am reading Against The Hounds of Hell: A Life of Howard Thurman by Peter Eisenstadt. I highly recommend the book. It is a definitive biography of one of the great spiritual leaders of our time. (Thurman’s most wellknown book, Jesus and the Disinherited, was, along with the Bible and United States Constitution, one of the three books that Martin Luther King Jr. carried with him when he traveled.) As the story of Thurman’s life unfolds, Eisenstadt describes the then 44-year-old pastor and scholar arriving in San Francisco in July 1944 after a five-day cross country train ride from Washington D.C. where he had been Dean of the Chapel at Howard University. After settling into a home that needed much care (think rodent infestation), Thurman began his work as the Senior Minister of the recently founded Church for the Fellowship of All People. Thurman told the church leaders that he wanted the church’s highest commitment to be to a peace rooted “in the quality of life that emanates from the place rather than from pronouncements of one kind or another.” His words describe my hope for this year’s celebration of AAHM. While it is important, especially in the face of efforts like those being made by Governor Ron DeSantis of Florida to deny the significance of African American history, that we make pronouncements about the significance of this celebration, the lessons we carry with us from the study of African American history are of greater significance than the statements we make about it. articles.text: On Monday, February 6, around 4 a.m., a 7.8 magnitude earthquake hit Turkey and Syria. The quake was the most powerful in the country since December 1939, when an earthquake of identical magnitude killed 30,000 people in December 1939. As of Tuesday afternoon, February 7, the death toll passed 7,200. The epicenter was 14.2 miles north of Nurdaği, a city in Gaziantep province, where southeastern Turkey borders northwestern Syria. Aftershocks ripped throughout the day and region; the strongest one measured a magnitude of 7.5, nine hours after and 59 miles north of the original epicenter. Tremors were felt as far away as Israel and Lebanon. Turkish President Recep Erdoğan declared a three-month state of emergency in 10 provinces affected by the earthquake. Turkey reported at least 5,434 deaths and 31,777 injuries. In government-controlled parts of Syria, at least 812 people were killed and 1,449 injured. Civil defense workers in the rebel-held northwest — which already faced a humanitarian crisis nearly 12 years into a bloody civil war — reported at least 1,020 deaths and 2,400 injuries. Thousands of buildings were flattened, leaving inhabitants homeless in near-freezing weather. Governments worldwide are pledging assistance and deploying aid as thousands of rescue workers desperately dig possible survivors from the rubble. The United States announced on Monday that it would deploy two specialized search-and-rescue teams of about 80 members each, one from Los Angeles and another from Virginia. Here are organizations working on rescue and recovery efforts. Donations are greatly needed. UNICEF The United Nations International Children’s Emergency Fund is in Syria and prioritizing water, sanitation, hygiene and nutrition, and focusing on helping unaccompanied children locate their families. UNICEF is accepting donations at unicefusa.org. Global Giving Global Giving, which helps local nonprofit agencies, is collecting donations at bit.ly/3DSf8JI to help fund emergency medical workers’ ability to provide food, shelter and medicine, among other necessities. As needs in Turkey and Syria change, the organization will focus on longterm assistance. The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies The IFRC is requesting donations for its Disaster Response Emergency Fund at bit.ly/3HFJe49 so it can send “immediate cash assistance.” OXFAM OXFAM, an international organization that fights poverty, is working with women’s cooperatives in Turkey to determine an appropriate immediate and longterm response plan. It is accepting donations at bit.ly/3YfjYso. CARE CARE, an organization that works with impoverished communities, is accepting donations that will go toward food, shelter and hygiene kits, among other items. Donate and learn more at bit.ly/3DRU3yO. Doctors Without Borders DWB, which responds to medical emergencies around the world, is collecting donations at bit.ly/3I7Jw5c. The Syrian American Medical Society SAMS is a United Statesbased humanitarian group that supplies medical care in Syria and nearby countries. At least one of its hospitals in northwestern Syria, Al Dana, received major damage, and SAMS collecting donations at bit.ly/3RJdBLz to deliver emergency aid. Save the Children Save the Children is accepting donations at bit.ly/3I6QmIb for its Children’s Emergency Fund, which will help provide children with food, shelter and warm clothing. The Union of Medical Care and Relief Organizations UOSSM, which since 2012 has provided medical relief and health care services inside Syria and to Syrian refugees in Turkey, is collecting money at https:// www.uossm.org/donate. Empowering the TurkishAmerican Community ETAC, a nonprofit which provides support services and guidance to members of the Turkish community with lack of means or language skills, is collecting donations which will be sent directly and entirely to rescue teams. Learn more and donate at bit.ly/3YeRz5W.

articles.text: Part 2 in a series Piedmont adults and youth have a wealth of opportunities to explore local volunteer work. Here are just a few. Mercy Brown Bag The Mercy Brown Bag program distributes well over one million pounds of food every year, thanks to hundreds of volunteers. The effort was launched in 1982 by residents at the Mercy Retirement & Care Center who saw that seniors in their Oakland neighborhoods were experiencing food insecurity. There are many ways to volunteer, including distributing lunch bags to homebound seniors, helping with special events or administrative tasks, helping at any of the 66 distribution sites throughout Alameda County, and translating written materials. Visit mercybrownbag.org/volunteer to learn more. Piedmont Community Service Crew Piedmont Community Service Crew (PCSC) is a coed youth-led organization under the auspices of the Piedmont Scout Council. It is the largest of the Venturing Crews with approximately 150 members, and actively seeks high school, middle school, and parent volunteers for ongoing programs. PCSC events and programs include meal preparation and cooking for low-income, elderly, and homeless members of the community; home renovation and environmental cleanup; and community engagement work such as youth tutoring. For more information on how to get involved, visit pcservicecrew.org. Asian Health Services Asian Health Services, located in Oakland, provides health, social, and advocacy services for all regardless of income, insurance status, immigration status, language or culture. The organization provides healthcare to more than 50,000 patients in English and over 14 Asian languages. Volunteers are critical to the center and contribute enormously to patients’ experiences. Opportunities are available in both clinical and non-clinical settings, including health education, fundraising, public relations, language access, administration, and midlevel or nurse practitioner positions. You must complete an online application. For more information, call (510) 986-6830, email hr@ ahschc.org, or visit asianhealthservices.org/volunteer-opportunities. Lake Merritt Institute Each month, thousands of pounds of trash accumulate in Lake Merritt. Lake Merritt Institute partners with local citizens and Oakland Unified School District students to help keep the lake’s shoreline and creeks clean on a weekly basis. Volunteers meet at the Institute office, on the shores of Lake Merritt, and usually work for between two and three hours during a shift. Training is provided, as are gloves, trash bags, barrels, nets, directions, and other materials. Cleanups are held five times a week during the school year and 3-4 times a week in the summer. Visit lakemerrittinstitute.org/how-youcan-help to learn more and sign up. Is there a volunteer effort or organization that you would like to highlight? Interested in expanding this list? articles.text: The February 1 edition of the Piedmont Post contained a story with a headline that bears clarification. Details in the story are correct, but the headline, “Fentanyl-laced drugs found in Piedmont,” more accurately would be, “Piedmont teen hospitalization attributed to Fentanyl.” The cursory testing of mushrooms confiscated by Piedmont Police did not show a trace of fentanyl. The confiscated drugs were sent to Alameda County for a full analysis. Results have not yet been received. The confirmation of fentanyl found in the blood of a Piedmont teenager, who was hospitalized and has fully recovered, comes from an article in The Piedmont Highlander, the school newspaper, and Piedmont School District-related emails. There is no evidence to show that fentanyl was purposefully ingested.

articles.text: The California Energy Commission approved Piedmont’s updated reach codes at their January 25 meeting, formalizing this set of local energy efficiency requirements for building projects that reach beyond statewide standards. Piedmont’s reach codes require that all new single-family homes and detached accessory dwelling units (ADUs) be all-electric. Additionally, the reach codes require energy efficiency measures be included in certain renovations to existing properties: • Electric panel replacements or upgrades must have capacity to accommodate future electrification of all appliances • Kitchen or laundry area renovation projects must install outlets that allow for the use of electric appliances in the future • Renovations or additions to existing homes that meet certain project value thresholds must incorporate one or more items from a menu of energy efficiency and electrification measures, such as installing insulation in attics or walls, replacing gas furnaces or water heaters with heat pump alternatives, or swapping incandescent light fixtures with LEDs • Projects that add a new upper level or increase the building’s roof area by 30% or more must install a photovoltaic (solar power) system Improving energy efficiency in existing buildings When Piedmont first adopted reach codes in 2021, it was one of the first cities in California to implement reach codes that apply to renovation projects in existing buildings in addition to new construction. Because the city is largely built out, improving energy efficiency in existing buildings is a critical part of meeting emissions reduction targets set in the city’s Climate Action Plan. Currently, natural gas use in residential buildings comprises about half of Piedmont’s in-territory greenhouse gas emissions. Reach codes, combined with other city initiatives like the recently launched home electrification rebate pilot program, play an important role in reducing the amount of energy used heating and cooling homes across Piedmont. Piedmont’s original reach codes have helped improve energy efficiency in over 150 home renovation projects. Changes in 2023 reach codes The updated reach codes are largely identical to the original set. Because reach codes are local amendments to statewide building codes, Piedmont must re-adopt its reach codes every time the State updates its building standards — which happens every three years. The most recent update to the State code took effect on January 1, 2023. Changes include: • minor terminology changes to align with updated language in the state code • increase in the project value thresholds that trigger reach codes for renovation projects, to accommodate rising construction costs • addition of a new energy efficiency measure (exterior wall insulation) to the menu of options for renovation projects Multifamily reach codes in development Existing reach codes apply only to single-family homes. The city is currently in the process of developing reach codes for multi-family properties. Community members can help inform what electrification and energy efficiency measures will be part of the multi-family reach codes by completing a brief online survey. The survey, found at bit.ly/3wWnegg, is available through March 1. For more information on reach codes, visit the city’s reach code webpage at bit.ly/ 3JA1Chs. For questions about the updated reach codes, contact Sustainability Program Manager Alyssa Dykman by email at sustainability@piedmont.ca.gov, or by phone at 420-3058. articles.text: Learn how you can make your home more energy efficient and get help paying for upgrades at a building electrification webinar presented by the City of Piedmont’s Sustainability Division tomorrow, Thursday, February 9 at 4 p.m. Replacing polluting gas appliances with clean, electric alternatives helps reduce greenhouse gas emissions from your home, improves indoor air quality, and saves money on energy bills. At the webinar, you’ll learn how to get started on electrifying your home, the types of electric appliances you’ll want to consider, and what rebate programs are available to help offset the costs of making these upgrades. Experts from the City of Piedmont, the Bay Area Regional Energy Network (BayREN), and local contractors will be on hand to answer questions. To attend the webinar, register online at: bit.ly/3DMNYng. Home electrification rebates The City of Piedmont launched a pilot rebate program for home electrification projects in January 2023, in hopes of encouraging more residents to make the switch to heat pump water heaters and high-efficiency heat pumps. Although upfront costs for such projects can be high, efficient heat pumps can lower energy bills dramatically, which results in significant savings over the long term. Traditionally, heating, ventilation, and air conditioning systems (HVAC) are the biggest home energy consumers, followed by water heating systems. For the average house, installing electric heat pumps in place of a gas furnace and gas water heater will reduce heating emissions by more than 45% over 10 years. Piedmont’s home electrification rebates help cover installation and labor costs on eligible projects and can be combined with other rebate programs such as those offered through BayREN. Qualified lower-income residents (those earning below $87,00 for a 2-person household) are eligible for double the standard rebate. Rebates are also available for service panel upgrades if they are necessary to support a qualified heat pump appliance. To be eligible for a rebate, upgrade projects must: • Replace an existing gas appliance • Be permanently installed and fixed to an existing single family or multifamily building • Have a City of Piedmont building permit submitted on or after January 3, 2023 • Be installed by a licensed contractor with an active City of Piedmont business license For program details and a full list of requirements, see the City’s Electrification Rebate Program Guide at bit.ly/40wZop6. The City Council has allocated $50,000 in funding for the rebate program pilot. Applications will be considered in the order they are received; the program will continue until funding is exhausted. For more information on the Electrification Rebate Program, see the City’s Rebates and Incentives webpage. With questions, contact Sustainability Program Manager Alyssa Dykman by email at sustainability@piedmont.ca.gov, or by phone at 420-3058.

articles.text: Piedmont Wellness Center will screen Like, a social media documentary aimed at pre-teens, teens and their families on Thursday, February 16, at 7 p.m. at the Alan Harvey Theater on the high school campus. The 50-minute documentary is focused on educating families about the impacts of social media. The screening is being co-hosted by the Wellness Center Support Committee and Piedmont Middle School. The screening was the brainchild of Piedmont Middle School counselor Amy Sharp. “We reached out to the Wellness Center Support Committee because we saw a lot come up with PMS students around social media during the past year. We were seeing instances of unkind and hurtful comments on digital platforms. The primary concern of showing the film was so that our students understand the harm being caused,” she said. The Wellness Center Support Committee responded immediately to the idea. “Counselors have front-row seats to the social-emotional challenges of our kids,” said Laurie Misra, a former Intern Therapist at the Wellness Center The Wellness Center, located at Piedmont High School, provides free mental health services to Piedmont students in middle school, Piedmont High, and Millennium High. So far this school year, students have visited the center well over 1,000 times. Under the supervision of two licensed psychologists, six intern therapists provide mental health support to Piedmont students, meeting once or twice for some or weekly with those who request it. Sharp said that outreach by the Wellness Center Support Committee has been incredibly helpful for the PMS counseling team. “They have been really proactive in reaching out to ask us how they can help,” she said. In the film Max Stossel, Head of Education Content for the Center for Humane Technology, says to the teen viewers, “These devices are not designed for you. You are not the customer; you are the product being sold here. Are you really using technology or is technology using you?”

articles.text: Through love, loss and flamboyant feather headdresses, this year’s high school musical, Hello, Dolly!, hit the stage of the Alan Harvey Theater for four evenings, February 2-5, with a flourish. Directed by PHS dance instructor Amy Moorhead, the show reprised the 1963 musical with brilliant costuming and lively acting and singing. Set in Yonkers, New York, in the early 20th century, the story follows the widowed matchmaker, Dolly Levi, on her own quest for love. Dolly is determined to marry a rich but ill-tempered client, Horace Vandergelder, for his money and money alone. However, in the end, she finds a relationship far more profitable than expected. PHS junior, Breah Bell, displayed exquisite vocal talent in the lead role, accompanied by senior Paden Andrews as Horace Vandergelder. While flashy and outgoing, the Hello, Dolly is very grounded and easy to relate to. “I think what makes Hello, Dolly such a classic and timeless musical, is that it’s so focused on human nature,” said Andrews, “the whole story is all about facing your own fear, and powering through and ‘rejoining the human race’ as Dolly says.” “[Dolly’s] personality matches with mine a lot. We’re both very outgoing and charismatic,” said Bell, “That makes it more enjoyable to play her.” Bell quickly credited the cast as her favorite part of putting on the musical. “Anyone considering going into show business, try out for the musical, any musical, any show, try it. articles.text: The start of a creative journey can happen at any second. It’s just about diving in and starting something new. But sometimes, getting started can feel incredibly daunting. We stop ourselves from trying new creative modalities because of fear of not being “good” or looking silly in front of our kids. Yet, research suggests that trying new things can have great benefits, including: improved memory, increased adaptability and better mood. A new creative activity could fit into a lot of different categories from music to visual art to crafting to baking. Recently, I decided to learn how to paint with gouache. To be clear, I don’t have a huge background in painting, but I have found that every time I play with a new medium I learn something about myself as a creator. It opens up curiosity and respect for artists who work in that medium or discipline. In the case of gouache, I was inspired because I learned that the original Disney animators who hand-painted the movie The Jungle Book used that medium. I have always been drawn into the richness and vibrancy of the colors used in that film. Bottom line: You don’t have to be an expert or a professional to benefit from playing with something new. It’s lovely to say “try something new,” but without inspiration it can feel nearly impossible. So, here are some ideas that might inspire your creative self and/or your creative family. Look at these prompts and just notice if anything comes to mind or sparks your interest. It doesn’t have to be literal, but just something that inspires you to make a connection. And then ask yourself, with this theme or idea, what kind of creative activity would you like to try for the first time? Poetry? Crochet? Oil Pastels? Crayon on Newspaper? • Shadow and Light • Bridge Over Nothingness • What’s at the End of the Rainbow? • Rhythms of Nature • Dragons vs. Unicorns • Your Tropical Island Awaits If none of these strike your fancy, try opening up any book to a random page and see what the first three words are that catch your eye. Then use those words as inspiration to just make something…anything! Have fun and create! Nina Meehan is a Creativity Consultant and speaker and former CEO of Nay Area Children’s Theatre. Find out more information about her work at gocreate. zone.

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ soccer team went into Friday’s match, February 3, against Castro Valley with its eyes on the prize. They knew that a win would mean clinching a berth in the North Coast Section post-season playoffs. Highly motivated, they put in perhaps their best performance of the season, defeating Castro Valley 5-0 at Witter Field before a hometown fan base. The victory improved Piedmont’s record to 7-1-5 overall and 5-1-4 in league (W-T-L) with just two matches left in the regular season. The final league games are tonight, Wednesday February 8 with Berkeley at Witter Field, and Friday at Encinal in Alameda. “I’m happy with how we played,” said veteran PHS coach Dan Chubbock after pinning a shutout on Castro Valley. “We created a lot of chances. We’ve been able to do all season, but we just haven’t been able to convert on a lot of them.. Tonight, we did. We didn’t want to let up,”. With 16 points toward the league table, Piedmont moved into second place (behind Berkeley’s 23 points) in the Western Alameda County Conference. Beating the Trojans was impressive considering Castro Valley entered Witter with a 10-4-5 record. But this time, CV rarely found a scoring opportunity in a game in which Piedmont put in a strong effort for the full 80 minutes. “We haven’t been getting the results we wanted. Tonight it felt like we finished our chances. We’re a really strong team, so it’s been frustrating because we’ve been playing well and just not getting the results we’ve been seeking. It felt good to get one back against a team we lost to earlier this season,” said senior leader Emily Fitzgerald. articles.text: Following the recent rainstorms, Cataract Falls on the north end of Mt. Tamalpais’ Cataract Creek is the most thriving it’s been in years. Arrive early to this bustling spot to avoid crowds. Throughout this hike, you will enjoy the pleasant sound of running water on a trail bordered by giant trees and shrubbery. The hike has two possible starting points. Beginning at the Cataract Trailhead on Fairfax-Bolinas Road, you will have a 2.8-mile out-and-back day with slightly over 1,000 feet in elevation gain. Beginning off of West Ridgecrest Blvd adds 0.8 miles to your hike, making a 3.6-mile round trip but still around 1,000 in ascent. The trail is lined with stairs that will give your lower body a good workout. Some of the steps require you to bring your knees up past your stomach – which can make it somewhat difficult for small dogs. Each step along the trail reveals some new variation on moss covered boulders and trees standing above you, while many old fallen trees hover above the creek and remain green year-round. The main attraction is the Helen Markt Falls about midway into your hike, where the cascade down Cataract Creek feeds beside a moss-covered boulder and into a pond. Helen Markt Falls is among the highlights of Cataract Falls Trail on Mt. Tamalpais. Staff photos Cataract Falls is a series of cascades that runs along the creek. Cataract Creek is picturesque with water flowing around moss-covered trees and stones.

articles.text: A memorial exhibition of the works of August Grahn will open at Piedmont Center for the Arts on Saturday, February 18, at 11 a.m. Born and raised in Piedmont, August Grahn was a student in Piedmont schools and an artist. He died in 2020 at the age of 26. The collection of art on display is representative of the work he did while attending the California Institute of the Arts (CalArts) in Santa Clarita from 2018 until his death. articles.text: Composer and conductor John Williams returns to Davies Symphony Hall to lead the orchestra on Valentine’s Day, February 14. This is the first time Williams has conducted the symphony in nearly a decade. He is joined by renowned violinist Anne-Sophie Mutter in a performance of Williams’ acclaimed Violin Concerto No. 2. Williams is an acclaimed composer best known for conducting well-known film scores. His career spans nearly seven decades and he has won 25 Grammy awards throughout his career. With over 50 Academy Award nominations, he is the second most nominated after Walt Disney. Mutter is a German violinist who worked under the legendary conductor Herbert von Karajan. She has had many pieces commissioned for her, including Williams’ work. The performance will include film music, with selections from some of Williams’ most popular film scores, such as Star Wars, Harry Potter, and Close Encounters of the Third Kind. articles.text: Vitamin Em is back in Piedmont for their Spring concert. The Grammy-nominated classical musicians with strong roots with Berkeley Symphony, bring their exciting range of crossover music to the PCA – from jazz to funk, classical to fiddle, soul to hip-hop. The audience will be treated to fearless improvisations. You’ve never heard music like this played by strings, bassoon and accordion. Featuring new works by Evan Price, Paul Hanson and Emily Onderdonk. Doors open at 3:30 p.m. Tickets $20 available in advance at https://www.vitaminemmusic.com/the-band/. $25 at the door. The program includes 5 arrangements by Emily Onderdonk: Hasse A’s: Arrangement of a Swedish fiddle Polska; very lively and rousing with elements that mimic guitars. Fancy Lady: A hip, soul tune based on the song of the same name by Billy Preston the great gospel and soul keyboardist. Tongue in Cheek: Written in a mixture of styles, including fiddle, rock, R&B and classical, featuring accordionist Dan Cantrel. Shake it Up: A fun, toe-tapping dance tune, in a 60’s pop style. Beautiful Child: Simple and heartfelt, dedicated to the memory of Emily’s brother, Matt, a wonderful musician who was a big influence on her love of the blues, rock, R&B and soul music. Seven Corners Country: An arrangement of the first song Paul Hanson wrote for his first album. This upbeat piece, generally in a jazz fusion style, includes Balkan and Bulgarian influences. articles.text: Review by Chris Honoré This family-friendly G-rated film opens with a red-haired girl (Francesca Capaldi) moving in across the street from Charlie Brown (Noah Schnapp). Of course, when Charlie gets his first glimpse of her, he is smitten and begins to plan how he can meet her. Naturally, the old gang is still around to offer their opinions to Charlie, and they haven’t changed. Lucy (Hadley Belle Miller) still thinks Chuck is a dufus, and Peppermint Patty (Venus Schulthels) hasn’t given up on hockey. When asked, she tells Charlie to keep his excitement about the red-haired girl to himself. Linus (Alexander Garfin) tells Charlie to simply walk across the street and introduce himself, while little sister Sally (Mariel Sheets) insists that Charlie’s new crush is not all that interesting. Snoopy (Bill Mendez), as always, is ready to support Charlie and he stands solidly at his side. The story is filled with flights of fantasy, especially when it comes to Snoopy’s dreams on top of his doghouse., He dreams of doing battle in the skis above France with his nemesis, The Red Baron. And for good measure, there’s the French poodle Fifi (Kristen Chenoweth), Snoopy’s imagined heartthrob. And not to forget Charlie’s trusty best bud Woodstock (also played by Mendez). There’s even a talent show for good measure, which offers Charlie the opportunity to demonstrate his essential kindness to his friends, despite his unresolved obsession with the red-haired girl. The animation is extraordinary with exceptional colors and background, The simple story is whimsical, warm, and there’s that familiar Chuck Brown selfdoubt, plus his haplessness and the fact that he can be his own worst enemy while always hoping for the best. This is demonstrated at a school pep rally where he wishes only that the red-haired girl will sit next to him. Later, on the school bus, she does sit next to Chuck, sending him into a panic, and causing him to crawl under his seat. The metaphor for all that occurs in a Peanuts’ story is Lucy holding the football for Charlie and pulling it away at the last moment, thus preventing Chuck from ever reaching his goal. He’s always trying, always sincere, and always vulnerable. The Peanuts Movie. Directed by Steve Martino. With voices of Noah Schnapp, Haley Belle Miller, and Mariel Sheets. 1 hr., 29 min. Rated G. articles.text: Lewis MacDougall in A Monster Calls Review by Chris Honoré A Monster Calls is extraordinary and a heartfelt surprise. But take seriously its rating of PG-13. While the trailer seems to promise a child’s tale, involving an enormous monster in the humanoid shape of gnarly yew tree, this British film is so much more. There is not a hint of Disney to be found, and the narrative goes far beyond the familiar “happily ever after”. Palliative. At the film’s center is 12-yearold Conor (Lewis MacDougall) who is in a place in his young life that is almost more than he can bear. He is relentlessly bullied at school, haunted by a traumatic nightmare that causes him to wake in the deep of night. He is coping with life-threatening cancer that is consuming his mother (Felicity Jones). He is unable to turn to his grandmother (Sigourney Weaver), who is rigid and distant. For most of his life his father (Toby Kebbell) has been absent. Though living in America, he arrives briefly due to his ex-wife’s illness, but offers little comfort to Conor. And then one night, as he sits in his room sketching in his notebook, strange things begin to happen, a pencil rolls across his desk, onto the floor. Things begin to move. And then, there, outside his opened window, stands a monster (the voice of Liam Neeson), a giant man-tree, who suddenly crashes into Conor’s room and speaks to him, insisting that he tell him three stories. Conor is both terrified and combative, wanting to suspend his disbelief yet boldly resistant to what is but cannot be. And so, just after midnight the monster returns and shares with Conor a fable that is gorgeously animated in watercolors (which are thematic throughout the film). The stories are puzzling, seemingly unrelated, and at first beyond Conor’s comprehension. And, as the monster points out, each is contradictory and are not what they seem. Meanwhile, Conor goes to school and deals with the bullies and attempts to cope with the reality that his mother is slipping away from him. Together the two of them cling to hope: his that she will live, that each new medical treatment will be a cure. Her hope is to prepare her son for what she knows will be. Deeply conflicted, Conor rages against the arc of his mother’s cancer, his anger uncontrollable, his helplessness ever with him. A Monster Calls is both a children’s allegory and an adult story. It is beautiful in its photography and in its narrative. It never backs away from the issues that young Conor is confronting. Tangentially, the monster demands that Connor tell him a fourth story that must be his own, one that the boy has refused to tell even himself. It is his deepest truth. The film, based on an idea offered by children’s author Siobhan Dowd just before she died, is realized in the 2011 award-winning book written by Patrick Ness. Conor is more a kid than an adult, and yet he stands at an intersection that is asks him to be both. And both is what A Monster Calls is all about. A Monster Calls. Directed by J.A. Bayona. 1 hr., 48 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2017. Now streaming on VUDU/ Prime/Netflix.

And then, there, outside his opened window, stands a monster (the voice of Liam Neeson), a giant man-tree, who suddenly crashes into Conor’s room and speaks to him, insisting that he tell him three stories. Conor is both terrified and combative, wanting to suspend his disbelief yet boldly resistant to what is but cannot be. And so, just after midnight the monster returns and shares with Conor a fable that is gorgeously animated in watercolors (which are thematic throughout the film). The stories are puzzling, seemingly unrelated, and at first beyond Conor’s comprehension. And, as the monster points out, each is contradictory and are not what they seem. Meanwhile, Conor goes to school and deals with the bullies and attempts to cope with the reality that his mother is slipping away from him. Together the two of them cling to hope: his that she will live, that each new medical treatment will be a cure. Her hope is to prepare her son for what she knows will be. Deeply conflicted, Conor rages against the arc of his mother’s cancer, his anger uncontrollable, his helplessness ever with him. A Monster Calls is both a children’s allegory and an adult story. It is beautiful in its photography and in its narrative. It never backs away from the issues that young Conor is confronting. Tangentially, the monster demands that Connor tell him a fourth story that must be his own, one that the boy has refused to tell even himself. It is his deepest truth. The film, based on an idea offered by children’s author Siobhan Dowd just before she died, is realized in the 2011 award-winning book written by Patrick Ness. Conor is more a kid than an adult, and yet he stands at an intersection that is asks him to be both. And both is what A Monster Calls is all about. A Monster Calls. Directed by J.A. The Peanuts Movie a small, enjoyable film Review by Chris Honoré This family-friendly G-rated film opens with a red-haired girl (Francesca Capaldi) moving in across the street from Charlie Brown (Noah Schnapp). Of course, when Charlie gets his first glimpse of her, he is smitten and begins to plan how he can meet her. Naturally, the old gang is still around to offer their opinions to Charlie, and they haven’t changed. Lucy (Hadley Belle Miller) still thinks Chuck is a dufus, and Peppermint Patty (Venus Schulthels) hasn’t given up on hockey. When asked, she tells Charlie to keep his excitement about the red-haired girl to himself. Linus (Alexander Garfin) tells Charlie to simply walk across the street and introduce himself, while little sister Sally (Mariel Sheets) insists that Charlie’s new crush is not all that interesting. Snoopy (Bill Mendez), as always, is ready to support Charlie and he stands solidly at his side. The story is filled with flights of fantasy, especially when it comes to Snoopy’s dreams on top of his doghouse., He dreams of doing battle in the skis above France with his nemesis, The Red Baron. And for good measure, there’s the French poodle Fifi (Kristen Chenoweth), Snoopy’s imagined heartthrob. And not to forget Charlie’s trusty best bud Woodstock (also played by Mendez). There’s even a talent show for good measure, which offers Charlie the opportunity to demonstrate his essential kindness to his friends, despite his unresolved obsession with the red-haired girl. The animation is extraordinary with exceptional colors and background, The simple story is whimsical, warm, and there’s that familiar Chuck Brown selfdoubt, plus his haplessness and the fact that he can be his own worst enemy while always hoping for the best. This is demonstrated at a school pep rally where he wishes only that the red-haired girl will sit next to him. Later, on the school bus, she does sit next to Chuck, sending him into a panic, and causing him to crawl under his seat. The metaphor for all that occurs in a Peanuts’ story is Lucy holding the football for Charlie and pulling it away at the last moment, thus preventing Chuck from ever reaching his goal. He’s always trying, always sincere, and always vulnerable. The Peanuts Movie. Directed by Steve Martino. With voices of Noah Schnapp, Haley Belle Miller, and Mariel Sheets. 1 hr., 29 min. Rated G. articles.text: Piedmonter Mary Geong became the first Asian president of Oakland Rotary Club #3 last summer. It is the third oldest in the world at 114 years and has 270 members. In the larger scheme, Oakland Rotary ranks 11th in total donations received out of the 36,000 clubs worldwide. Geong’s path to her presidency began in 2002, when she joined the Rotary Club with the encouragement of friend and fellow CPA Chris Yahng, the first Asian president of the CalCPA society in its 100-year history. Geong’s rise to the top is even more impressive when considering that females were allowed to become members in the Rotary Club only after a 1989 Supreme Court ruling. Geong and friend Mary Liu, the first female Asian president of San Francisco Rotary Club #2 in 2021, refer to their roles as “breaking the bamboo ceiling.” Geong, a leader of the Piedmont Asian American Club for more than 25 years, hosted a Lunar New Year dinner at Peony seafood restaurant in Oakland’s Chinatown, on January 26, and invited Liu’s San Francisco Mary Geong who was born in Guangzhou, China is pictured with new Oakland mayor Sheng Thao. Geong presents a grant of $7,329 to St. Vincent de Paul of Alameda County. Mary Geong, president of Oakland Rotary Club #3, gives a speech at the Rotary Club Lunar New Year dinner on January 26. Rotary Club #2 and the San Francisco Chinatown Rotary Club to attend. The result was a turnout of 114 people The same three Rotary clubs joined forces last summer to hand out over 600 personal safety alarm kits to seniors in Oakland’s Chinatown after anti-Chinese attacks on seniors made national news. Geong’s focus with the Rotary Club continues to be education. Each year the club awards up to 10 scholarships of $10,000 to Oakland students who will be attending college. The Rotary Club follows up with the recipients by providing one-on-one mentorship during their college years. Another large effort taken by the Geong-led club is supporting the expanding Transitional Kindergarten (TK) program for four-year-olds. The club donates three books to every (TK) student in Oakland School District and gives each teacher a $250 gift card to buy supplies for the class. The club also sponsors field trips annually to Fairyland and the Oakland Zoo for TK students. “We feel that education is a way for anybody to move forward and upward. I was one of the first in my family to go to college, and because of college I’ve been able to succeed,” explained Geong. As president, Geong prepares the budget of the Oakland Club for its philanthropy, and allocates funds to all its committees. While much of the work is local, the Oakland Rotary Club is involved internationally and provides funding for projects on five continents. “Most Rotary clubs are in two or three continents, we are in five. That makes us unique and that’s never occurred in our 114 years,” she said. Individual Oakland Rotary Club members donated $15,000 to Ukraine after the war began, and the club matched that amount. Geong’s status as president highlights the start, not the end, of the diversity work that she wants to see happen within the Rotary Club. While female members make up roughly half the membership now, Asians make up only 10%. “We need some more work in that area to encourage more people of different ethnic groups to match the city of Oakland’s demographics,” said Geong. Geong invites all Piedmonters and anyone interested in making a difference to attend Rotary Club’s annual Gala on May 4 at the Sequoia Country Club. articles.text: Oakland Museum of California began its popular White Elephant Sale on January 29 with a sold-out crowd of enthusiastic “Preview” shoppers. The sale, which benefits the Museum, will have a series of shopping days in February and culminate with a final “Blow Out Sale” on March 4 and 5. All events require tickets but the final weekend is free of charge. To purchase tickets see: www. whiteelephantsale.org. It takes generous donors, loyal customers, and dedicated volunteers to make the White Elephant Sale a success. One Piedmont resident, Sandra Cook, can claim to have done all three of these “jobs”. A resident of Piedmont for 44 years, she has been shopping at the sale for over 20 years and began working as a volunteer cashier in 2022. When she found out the volunteer commitment was year-round, she offered to help in the Boutique Department which sells fine china, glassware She spends most of her time processing packaging materials for reuse. “We reuse all the packing material. articles.text: Did you know that Piedmont is buying 100% California wind and solar power? The city is being served by East Bay Community Energy (EBCE), a not-for-profit public agency providing sustainable power to customers in Alameda County. I spoke with Kelly Birdwell Brezovec, Director of Account Services at EBCE and a Piedmont resident, about how EBCE serves customers and the environment. EBCE is what’s called a Community Choice Aggregation (CCA). “CCAs have been around for more than ten years in the state of California, enabled by a piece of legislation that allowed the development of these programs within communities to provide local control and an energy mix that more closely matches the demands or the requests of the population,” said Brezovec. With EBCE, residents have the option to power their homes sustainably. “We offer our customers a really easy way to be served by 100% renewable energy,” said Brezovec. Piedmont was the first city in Alameda County to default municipal and residential customers to the Renewable 100 plan — 100% California solar and wind energy — which aligns with Piedmont’s Climate Action Plan goals. In addition to benefiting the environment, EBCE can also save customers money if they choose to enroll in the Bright Choice plan, priced 3% below PG&E rates. EBCE estimates that its Bright Choice customers save $19 million each year compared to what they would have paid PG&E. EBCE’s Board of Directors comprises local elected officials and Piedmont’s mayor has a seat on the board. Starting March 1, Councilmember Betsy Anderson will represent Piedmont. “You can be in touch with a local city council member and voice your opinion. You can also join our public board meetings and make a public comment,” Brezovec said. Because EBCE is not-forprofit, they reinvest earnings back into the community. “We offer community sponsorships of up to $2500 to local organizations like youth sports teams, social services, and stem programs,” said Brezovec. In 2020, the Piedmont Makers Robotics Team received a sponsorship. In addition to community groups and businesses, EBCE supports local governments with technical and financial assistance. Last year, EBCE assisted Piedmont in conducting a municipal fleet electrification study and provided gap funding to replace all remaining gas water heaters in municipal buildings with energy-efficient heat pump water heaters. The city is also working with EBCE to install the city’s first publicly accessible electric vehicle DC fast chargers near the Exedra.

articles.text: Joe Cross Creason III, known as Cross, passed away suddenly on the morning of January 27, 2023 at his family home in Piedmont. He was 52 years old. While the glow of his brilliance and caring heart faded far too soon from this world, he lived a life of passions, achievements and dedication that we will always remember. Born in San Francisco on June 22, 1970, he lived the first years of his life with his mother and father before moving to Piedmont where he was soon joined by a sister, Winnie. Cross attended Piedmont schools from preschool through Middle School. He graduated from high school at College Preparatory School in Oakland. Furthering his education, Cross attended the University of California, Santa Barbara, then graduated from the University of California, Davis. He gained a law degree from the McGeorge School of Law, in Sacramento, where he was a staff writer for the Law Review and earned numerous scholastic honors, including three American Jurisprudence Awards, as well as being a member of the Roger J. Traynor Honor Society and the Order of the Coif. For over 20 years, Cross practiced law in San Francisco at the law firm of Dillingham and Murphy, where he was a partner. Cross was a true Renaissance man with an expansive intellect and curiosity. He immersed himself in each of his interests in order to obtain a level of ability and knowledge that would have been impressive for the focus of just a single subject. There was hardly a string instrument that Cross didn’t know how to play. His musical passions started as a child with the bass and guitar, before expanding his abilities to the ukulele, banjo, mandolin and others later in life. Cross’s language skills were as impressive as his musical talents. He was a fluent Spanish speaker and read a range of books from novels to non-fiction in the language. Cross had expanded his repertoire to include parts of Mandarin and French as well. He was a gifted writer and lover of literature. Cross enjoyed an eclectic group of authors including Faulkner and Asimov. He was deeply informed on history and politics. He closely followed debates regarding public policy and played a limited but Alice Creason with son Cross Creason, grandson Joe Creason, and daughter Winnie Creason in 2002. Cross Creason with son Joe Creason on Joe’s 1st Birthday in 1999. Cross Creason engaged role in local politics in Alameda County where he had resided for over 10 years. A life-long sports enthusiast and excellent athlete, Cross was a talented tennis player and former member of the Berkeley Tennis Club. More recently he had taken up the sport of pickleball, displaying his advanced skills and superior strokes, as well as returning to golf. He was a longtime basketball player, following in the footsteps of his father and winning a CIF title for College Prep during his senior year in 1988. Piedmont basketball courts were a favorite of his, where he frequently shot baskets and played pickup games. On weekends Cross enjoyed cooking using various techniques, cooking methods, and cookbooks as he carefully learned new recipes. Cross also had a green thumb and was able to produce beautiful vegetables and seasonings for his dishes. Cross loved his son, Joe Cross Creason IV, very much. They played guitar, hiked in the Oakland hills, and kayaked in the Bay. Cross leaves behind many family members, his mother Alice Creason, sister Winnie Creason, Son Joe Creason, wife Tiffany Sun, stepson Joshua Gu, aunt Estelle Hood, uncle William Creason, aunt Louise Creason, and cousins Hunt Cochrane and Harriet, Herbert Cochrane and Posey, Philippe Patat, Scott Creason and Mollie, Lyman Creason and Sharon, and many more. He was 52 years old. While the glow of his brilliance and caring heart faded far too soon from this world, he lived a life of passions, achievements and dedication that we will always remember. Born in San Francisco on June 22, 1970, he lived the first years of his life with his mother and father before moving to Piedmont where he was soon joined by a sister, Winnie. Cross attended Piedmont schools from preschool through Middle School. He graduated from high school at College Preparatory School in Oakland. Furthering his education, Cross attended the University of California, Santa Barbara, then graduated from the University of California, Davis. He gained a law degree from the McGeorge School of Law, in Sacramento, where he was a staff writer for the Law Review and earned numerous scholastic honors, including three American Jurisprudence Awards, as well as being a member of the Roger J. Traynor Honor Society and the Order of the Coif. For over 20 years, Cross practiced law in San Francisco at the law firm of Dillingham and Murphy, where he was a partner. He immersed himself in each of his interests in order to obtain a level of ability and knowledge that would have been impressive for the focus of just a single subject. articles.text: Vandals invaded the nativeplant nursery, Friends of Sausal Creek, in Joaquin Miller Park on Friday, January 24, throwing thousands of plants to the ground, smashing pots and overturning tables and benches. The preliminary damage estimates ranged from $4,500 to $7,000. The event mirrored a few of the experiences that Piedmont Scouts have experienced with their service projects. Scouts with Troop 6 have performed many service projects at Sausal Creek. Piedmont Scout Council President Lisa Gros, also a longtime leader with Troop 6, said, “The vandalism was indicative of one of the things we try to counteract in Scouts. We try to foster the ‘we’ instead of the ‘me.’ I hope that this was an isolated incident and not a bigger issue where people are caring more about whatever they want than what’s good for the broader community.” Gros’ son Jack encountered vandalism only a few days after the construction of his Eagle Scout project in May 2019, a Graffiti on the fence at the El Centro Trailhead of the Dimond Canyon Trail by Sausal Creek 160-foot fence at the El Centro Trailhead of the Dimond Canyon Trail, protecting the genetically pure trout native to Sausal Creek. The fence was damaged with graffiti and completely torn down in some sections. Gros speculated that a few homeless people were living up the hill on the other side of the canyon and possibly broke the Two Scouts from Troop 6 repair the broken fence. fence. “The Scouts do things like this to better their community, and it’s a shame that not everyone appreciates that intent,” said Gros. Since then, parts of the fence were washed out in the recent winter storms. The fence, and other Troop 6 projects, are intended to protect the parklands of the Oakland Hills from erosion. Toward that end, many Troop 6 projects involve replanting the hillsides with native-plant life, in collaboration with Wendy Tokuda, a former Piedmont resident and TV news anchor, who now leads many environmental restoration efforts under Friends of Sausal Creek. Throughout Gros’ seven-year involvement with Friends of Sausal Creek, Troop 6 Scouts have been working with Tokuda to stabilize native plant life, clear potentially flammable redwood debris, and clear the trail. “If the Sausal Creek damages were really only $7,000,” said Gros, “someone could open their wallet.
